Q: How do I clone a subdirectory only of a Git repository? A:

Use:

git init <repository>
cd <repository>
git remote add origin <URL>
git config core.sparsecheckout true
echo "<path you want to clone>/*" >> .git/info/sparse-checkout
git pull --depth=1 origin <branch you want to fetch>

An example for cloning only the Jetsurvey folder from this repository:

git init MyFolder
cd MyFolder
git remote add origin git@github.com:android/compose-samples.git
git config core.sparsecheckout true
echo "Jetsurvey/*" >> .git/info/sparse-checkout
git pull --depth=1 origin main

Q: How to correctly activate micromamba environment inside Apptainer container automatically? A:

I've encountered a similar frustrating issue and have spent almost a day now reading and trying different solutions. I've seen this sort of solution come up a few times, but it's not ideal for me because it won't actually initialize micromamba and won't actually activate the environment in the singularity exec and singularity shell use cases. I think you'll have access to the packages from your environment, but you want be able to deactivate and switch enviornments, etc.

I think the best answer out there is here. As the answer says, the key thing is that by defining SINGULARITY_SHELL, we are bypassing the --norc flag and allowing the intialize and activation steps in the /etc/bash.bashrc to occur. Credit goes to the author of that answer, my only contribution is bring attention to their great solution and I would add the code below to the end of the environment section, so that way you can see the active environment in the prompt at first launch.

%environment
    # Add the following to the END of the envirnoment section to get a nice command prompt at first launch
    export CONDA_PROMPT_MODIFIER="(name_of_your_env_you_want_at_launch) "
    export PS1="${CONDA_PROMPT_MODIFIER}Apptainer> "

Q: How to convert quadratic bezier curve code into cubic bezier curve? A:

If the animated diagram in the original answer is difficult to understand, this might be easier to see.

In a cubic Bézier curve, a linear interpolation is applied first on each line segment connecting the four control points to then produce three intermediate points.

A second interpolation is then applied on each line segment connecting those three intermediate points, producing a point on each.

Afterward, an interpolation between those two new points produces a point on the curve.

Q: How to recognize if a string contains unicode chars? A:

Starting with .NET 6 you may use Char.IsAscii(char c):

Returns true if c is an ASCII character ([ U+0000..U+007F ]).
Per https://www.unicode.org/glossary/#ASCII, ASCII is only U+0000..U+007F.

So, for an entire string, you could introduce an extension method such as:

public static class StringExtensions
{
    public static bool IsAscii(this string s) => s?.All(Char.IsAscii) ?? false;
}

The definition of ASCII used Char.IsAscii() is consistent with that used by Encoding.ASCII so if you are trying to test whether a string could be encoded to ASCII without actually constructing the resulting byte array, this is the correct way to do it.

Q: HTTP/2 requests to Spring Boot on ECS behind AWS NLB fail with PROTOCOL_ERROR (HTTP/1.1 works fine) A:

Answering my own question here to document this somewhere. Hopefully it will help sombody. We tracked this down to a new validation in the Tomcat version that ships with Spring Boot 4.1.0.

Root cause

With an NLB doing TLS offload, the client connects over HTTPS but the connection from the NLB to the backend is plain (non-TLS). When HTTP/2 is in use, the original :scheme pseudo-header (https) is still forwarded to the backend. HTTP/1.1 has no such pseudo-header, which is why HTTP/1.1 traffic was unaffected.

In April, Tomcat added a check that the HTTP/2 :scheme pseudo-header is consistent with whether TLS is actually enabled on the connector. The relevant commit is apache/tomcat@81712d2. If the incoming scheme is https but the connector does not have SSL enabled (our case, since the backend connection is plain), Tomcat rejects the stream with a PROTOCOL_ERROR / RST.

That commit was released as part of Spring Boot 4.1.0 on June 10th, so the breakage showed up the moment we upgraded.

How we found it

We took a tcpdump of the traffic between the NLB and the container. Seeing https in the forwarded :scheme against a plainly non-TLS hop is what pointed us at the consistency check.

We could then reproduce it locally by sending an HTTP/2 request with a :scheme of https over a plain connection, which fails the same way:

❯ curl --http2 --http2-prior-knowledge http://localhost:8080/actuator/health -H ':scheme: https'
curl: (92) HTTP/2 stream 1 reset by server (error 0x1 PROTOCOL_ERROR)

The fix we went with

We made the path to the container actually use TLS, so the forwarded :scheme: https is now consistent with the transport. This means configuring the NLB target group to use TLS (re-encryption) and serving TLS on the container.

A useful detail: the certificate on the container can be self-signed. In our experience the NLB re-encrypts to the target without requiring the target's certificate to chain to a trusted CA. From the AWS documentation:

If a target group is configured with the TLS protocol, the load balancer establishes TLS connections with the targets using certificates that you install on the targets. The load balancer does not validate these certificates. Therefore, you can use self-signed certificates or certificates that have expired. Because the load balancer is in a virtual private cloud (VPC), traffic between the load balancer and the targets is authenticated at the packet level, so it is not at risk of man-in-the-middle attacks or spoofing even if the certificates on the targets are not valid.

An alternative we tried but didn't keep

We also tried setting SSLEnabled="true" on the Tomcat connector without configuring real TLS settings. This makes the connector report itself as SSL-enabled, so the :scheme consistency check passes and the error goes away. It worked, but we weren't really comfortable with this because it might cause problems in the future (?). In the past it was common to set the secure property if proxying to the backend, and that just seems to be metadata on the request when querying HttpServletRequest#isSecure(), but I'm not so sure about setting SSLEnabled. Again, it works, but YMMV.
